subtopic: REPORTED EMPLOYMENT AT CHURCHILL OF WORKERS FROM EASTERN CANADA
speechtext:
All right. If it comes
to a matter of asking a question, I can soon do that. The question is this: Is it true that workers from eastern Canada are being sent to Churchill? This article states that unemployed men paraded at the Pas as a demonstration against eastern workers being sent to that part of Manitoba. I should like to know if that has been done, because this is a question of interest to the whole of western Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
subtopic: REPORTED EMPLOYMENT AT CHURCHILL OF WORKERS FROM EASTERN CANADA
speechtext:
I am rather glad the hon. member has brought up this question, because during the last few hours I have been inundated with this statement from various people in the west. I see according to one newspaper sent me that Premier Bracken made the statement that large numbers of men were being taken to Churchill from the east, and the mayor of The Pas is reported to have made a similar statement. I was looking into the matter, without knowing anyone was going to bring it up, so I think I can give a fairly intelligent answer.
The number of men taken to Churchill as working on the line from The Pas to Churchill amounts to approximately one thousand, but of that number about one half are men who have been in there for a number of

years, who have some special qualifications and who have been reemployed. In round figures, some four hundred men I am informed have been taken from The Pas, or about a third of the total number employed. The men taken from other sections of the country, and certainly those taken from the east, with very rare exceptions, were men who had been there in previous years and who had some special qualifications. There were some men taken from Renfrew county, men who have been there for a number of years. They are called adze men; they have special qualifications for working timber. Other men were taken from the maritime provinces; they were steamship men, who have been there for some years. I do not think the numbers of these men have been increased.
With regard to The Pas, there is no doubt that many men went there looking for work this year. I am informed by people in the west that hundreds of men vrent to The Pas on freight trains and in other ways, in the hope of getting work. Of course it is impossible for the Department of Railways and Canals to supply work for all these men. They went in on their own. responsibility, and we have taken as many as we can take. Probably 90 per cent of all the employees on the line from The Pas to Churchill and at Churchill have been taken from Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and I think that is a very fair proportion.
There may be very good arguments advanced in support of the contention that men should not be brought from other sections of Canada, but only those men who have special training or who had previous knowledge of the work were taken from other parts of the country, and their numbers are very small. I think it well that this fact should be made known to the people of western Canada. I can assure my hon. friend and the country that The Pas and western Canada have been treated very fairly in this matter. It may be pointed out that Winnipeg, for instance, has thousands of men unemployed. We did take perhaps 150 men from Winnipeg, but surely that city has some right to be considered. There were a few men taken from Regina, a few from Selkirk and a few from various other sections, and I may say that I was approached from all over western Canada, asking me for positions at Churchill. I suppose for each position we had to offer there were from ten to twenty applications.

subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS

speakeroldname: Mr. H. E. SPENCER (Battle River) moved:
subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this-house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of carrying into effect the decision of parliament made on the 3rd March, 1930, to make grants to the provinces equal to one-third of cost of establishing, and to cover permanently, such full time health units as may be organized.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, a year ago I had
the pleasure of introducing in this house a resolution somewhat similar to the one we are considering to-day. That resolution read:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of making grants to the provinces equal to one-third the cost of establishing, and to cover permanently, such full time health units as may be organized.
During the discussion, which I am glad to say was participated in by hon. members from various parts of the house, every one of the seventeen members who took part was favourable to the resolution, and the result was that the house unanimously endorsed the principle. The question might well be asked: If that were the case last year, why bring a similar motion to the house again this year? I do so for the simple reason that since that time we have had a change of government, and although the members of the present government were very sympathetic to the resolution I introduced a year ago when they were in opposition, I thought it just as well to test out their opinion now that they are in office.
To-day, both in provincial and federal legislation, we are giving consideration to many things that were at one time left to the individual. One of those subjects of course, is that of education. We realized that education is a national asset, and we make it compulsory that alb boys and girls shall devote so many years of their lives to acquiring an education of some sort. We are now more and more coming to the opinion, generally speaking, that health should be put on exactly the same basis as education, that the health of the nation is a national asset, and that its care cannot be left entirely, as has been too much the case in the past, to the individual. In world competition to-day an unhealthy nation can no more compete against a healthy nation than can an ignorant nation stand up against a well-educated one. It is with that idea in mind that I am bringing forward this resolution in the hope that the government will

National Health
' look upon it as sympathetically to-day as they did when in opposition and assist in carrying out the proposals that I am putting forward.
Speaking in support of a resolution with regard to health some weeks ago, I mentioned that to-day the health of a man and his family is governed practically by the length of his purse, if he has any purse at all. One hon. member on the other side of the house who happened to be of the medical profession said in reply that he did not think that such was the case. He felt that the medical profession generally never hesitated to take care of the sick when they needed care, whether they had any more money or not. I am proud to be able to say that I think that is so in most cases, but unfortunately there are cases, and I have come across them, where the medical official does not always take that generous attitude. I well remember the case of a family in 1918 during the flu epidemic. This family was attended by a medical practitioner, but as soon as he found out that they had no money and that he was not likely to get paid, he left instructions with them how to take care of themselves and said that he was too busy to come again. But just as soon as the municipality decided to guarantee all the medical bills of those who were suffering from influenza, this same practitioner came back and continued to visit the family regularly. The same man told a friend of mine that if the flu had lasted for only two years more, he would have been in a position to retire for good. I just throw that out in answer to the criticism of my statement that was made the other day.
Under present conditions, too many people, fearing the cost of medical or hospital care, put off calling in the necessary medical assistance until it is too late. It is to get around this difficulty that I am proposing this resolution to the house. Through preventive medicine a lot of people can be guarded against sickness. That is much better than allowing themselves to become ill, and then attempting a cure.
I am very glad to give praise to the splendid work that has been carried on by the Canadian Social Hygiene Council in educating the people throughout this country to the importance of taking care of health. Many organizations are engaged in health educational work, and many suggestions are being made. The one before us to-day is that of the full time health unit. This system of preventive medicine, of course, has been very successful indeed in the United States, where they have between 300 and 400 health units, working with splendid results. This system
has been encouraged in this country and elsewhere. Some parts of this country have taken advantage of the offer of the Rockefeller Foundation, which very generously provides one-third of the cost of these health units for the first three years. When they .have been going three years and the Rockefeller Foundation steps out, according to the agreement, the extra expense has to be taken care of locally by the provincial government or some other body, and what I am asking in this resolution is that the federal government shall assume its share and bear one-third of the cost of these full time health units.

subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext: After the first three years?

subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
Yes.
Sickness is not local or provincial; it is interprovincial, and as the federal government look after various matters of interprovincial concern, I ask that they assume the responsibility of looking after one-third of the cost of these health units for the purpose of preventing sickness, because sickness so far as we are concerned is interprovincial. The various provinces of Canada have begun to organize to a considerable extent full time health units. The province of Quebec has been ahead of all the rest. It has to-day twenty-three health units, and is organizing three more. British Columbia has five, and is very enthusiastic indeed over their success already; Alberta is organizing two health units this year.
As to the cost of these organizations, I was reading some literature from the province of Quebec this morning, which shows that the average cost of a health unit is from $12,000 to $13,000, and they are serving anywhere from 15,000 to 53,000 people, according to the density of the population.
I should like to quote from a letter that I received the other day from Dr. H. E. Young, who is a provincial health officer for British Columbia. He sent me a booklet on health, and he says:
On page 41 there is an account of the Saanich unit, the first one established. I would particularly call your attention to the improvement in school attendance, the correc-;ipn of defects and the saving in money, particularly in regard to the amount of money saved as a result of our work in reference to retarders, or what may be called the cost of educating children who have to repeat grades. You will note that while retardation cost Saanich $17,000 in 1928, the cost was reduced to $11,000 in 1929, and this has been further cut down to $600 in 1930. This has been largely due to our work in conjunction with the inspector of schools, who is a very able man. This has been a remarkable saving in cost.
National Health

He says further:
t 1 have not a printed report of North Vancouver health unit, which was opened last September, but the response of the people after the first few months of operation has been wonderful.
The letter ends as follows:
We began this work in the autumn of 1927 and the results have more than justified our predictions. In a unit the work is consolidated, the nurses are well trained, the medical man in charge does not practise, but devotes his whole time to preventive work, and the people are realizing the real purport of our efforts, and public education on health matters is progressing in a most satisfactory manner.
There is so much good material from which I could draw for the purposes of this address I find some difficulty in knowing what to leave out. I wish particularly to put on record a statement made by Sir William Arbuthnot Lane which deals specially with preventive medicine. Sir William Arbuthnot Lane was one of the foremost physicians and surgeons of Great Britain. He pointed out the folly of the present system of treating the sick instead of saving lives by the prevention of disease. The quotation is as follows:
The great development of the future in medicine, as I see it, will lie in the scrapping of present ideas and the concentrating upon keeping people fit and enabling them to build up physical power and energy to resist disease.
And the quotation goes on as follows:
More and more doctors are beginning to realize that it is archaic folly to treat only the sick.
I am informed by medical men that such diseases as diphtheria, typhoid fever and scarlet fever are largely preventable. Yet in spite of this fact great numbers die annually of these diseases. To give some idea of the extent to which these diseases may be controlled, I find by records which I trust are correct, that during the war period typhoid was so controlled that from this disease we did not lose a single Canadian soldier in France. We find from the records that within a period of one year tuberculosis is responsible for the death of over 7,000 people. Yet, according to literature put out by the Canadian Social Hygiene Council this disease could be completely eliminated by the exercise of health control. Similar figures are available with respect to cancer and heart disease. I think, however, for my purposes the figures I have quoted are sufficient. In closing I should like to quote from one of the addresses given in the house about a 'year ago. Hon. members will recall that the then Minister of Finance, although speaking in support of the resolution, simply asked the

question: "From where is the money to come"? At this time I am going to quote from the remarks of the right hon. gentleman *who is now the Finance minister. Speaking in the debate which took place on March 3 last year the Hon. R. B. Bennett made the following statement, as at page 234 of Hansard:
Touching the necessity for the establishment of health units nothing need be said; I think the case is complete almost before it is stated.
At a later stage he said:
"A nation's health is a nation's wealth." We as a parliament are concerned in the health of the Canadian people as a whole. To the extent to which men are able to labour, free from disease, we have added to the national wealth; to the extent which citizens by studying preventive medicine obtain knowledge, from clinics and other methods, for which the nation might *well pay, we have added to the national wealth of Canada.
And, further he states:
We are asked merely to make a grant in aid of the effort which the provinces will carry forward to ensure the health of the Canadian people as a whole, not provincially but nationally, not in a narrow and circumscribed area but throughout this Dominion as a whole, in order that the knowledge of preventive medicine may become universal and in order that the greatest means known to man to increase the national wealth, namely, measures to ensure the national health of our people, may become an accomplished fact.
1 am in support of this resolution for that reason.
Those were the words of the present Prime Minister of this country. I have not the slightest doubt that he believes the same today. I know that he is very much interested in the subject of health, because for some years he was closely connected with the work of the Red Cross. Whether or not we may agree with him concerning certain subjects we recognize that our present Prime Minister is a man of action. Having heard his words last year, I hope he will this year repeat them. In view of the fact that he holds the most important portfolio, that of finance, I hope he will see his way clear again to support this resolution which was so well supported last year by hon. members behind him.

subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
I rise to support the principle of this resolution because if adopted it will carry to the door steps of the people of this country the very

National Health
best that has been learned along the lines of preventive medicine. I believe the suggestion is sound in theory, reasonably easy of application and possible under present financial conditions. If adopted it will represent. a progressive step toward a more even distribution of the benefits of the best that the age affords in the way of preventive medicine and health insurance. Every province has done much to assist in curing disease. For instance, the province of Alberta has encouraged the building of twenty-two municipal hospitals and pays grants to eighty-seven approved hospitals. That province supports a provincial sanatarium and was the first to construct a special hospital for the treatment of infantile paralysis. Those of us who know about the deformities left by this dread disease will be most enthusiastic in the support of this movement. That province also provides some physicians in outlying rural districts, and travelling clinics do mutch to provide dentistry and minor operations for people in districts who otherwise would not receive such care. A health unit is something which will appeal to the people who dread or shrink from the necessity of travelling long distances or going among strangers to receive advice or care. The health unit would bring to the homes of the people the advice they are entitled to receive.
What is a health unit? In Alberta there is a proposal to establish two units during the present year, one at Red Deer, and one at High River. The total cost is expected to reach about $10,000 or $12,000 per year. The Rockefeller Institute will provide one-quarter of the sum for the period of three years, the province will provide one-half and the remaining quarter will be raised by the municipalities included in the unit. The staffs have already been appointed consisting of a medical officer specially qualified in public health work, a sanitary inspector, a secretary and a public health nurse. This is not some new or untried venture. Health units have proven their usefulness for a period of twenty years. The first unit was established in Yakima county in 1910 and there are now 500 health units in the United States. Quebec has twenty-three, Saskatchewan has two, New Brunswick three or four and British Columbia four.
Now, briefly what is the work of these health units? It falls naturally under four heads. The first is child welfare, and has to do with examination of school children and children of pre-school age. Are hon. members aware that thirty out of every hundred children attending school have defective eyesight?
This is often neglected and it results in much sorrow and much discomfort later in life. A large number of children have diseased tonsils and teeth, defective heart and lungs, and suffer from malnutrition. These health units will have officers right on the ground who will go to the homes and talk to the parents on the disabilities that their children are labouring under and advise them as to the best means of obtaining treatment. The second division of this work covers control of contagious diseases. Something has been said about the prevention of diphtheria, smallpox and scarlet fever. It has been stated on good authority that diphtheria and scarlet-fever should be unknown in the next generation of children, there being methods of immunization which in the great majority of cases will prevent these diseases. The health unit also takes control of venereal disease, tuberculosis and infantile paralysis. Certainly this offers a great field of activity, and if the work is properly conducted it will bring glorious results. The third heading has to do with public health education, that is, sanitary inspection, testing of water supply and food, vital statistics, disposal of sewage, as well as education along the lines of cleanliness.
I have left to the last perhaps the most important work which could be done locally by a health clinic; I refer to life extension work. In one of these districts there are probably 3,600 school children, and the activities of the health unit would effect a saving of $1,800 right there. What are the causes of sudden death among men and women during the years of their active life? Tuberculosis is no longer the dreaded disease that it once was, but there is still a great deal of mortality attributable to heart disease, kidney trouble and diabetes. What are the causes of these deaths? Some are caused by complications resulting from infectious diseases suffered in childhood. Many deaths are caused by improper habits of living, by unwise diet, and by the presence of infectious foci which are slowly poisoning the system. Where is the man or woman approaching fifty who should be examined to see if any of these diseases are present in their early stages? Acting on what such an examination discloses the proper means of treatment may be taken advantage of. We hear of the sudden death of many people at fifty and onwards, and I am convinced that a little money spent in encouraging the establishment of health units would do much to prevent this mortality, because appropriate treatment could be taken in time to eradicate or control the trouble.
National Health

It used to be said, "If you wish to be healthy go to the country." That advice does not apply at the present time because the death rate in the country is 8 per cent in excess of that in the cities. Modern preventive medicine has done much to lower the death rate in urban centres. Due to sickness and disease we have an economic loss of $300,000,000 a year. We do much to prevent fire hazards. Surely we should do much more to prevent premature death and thus preserve -the precious asset of healthy people. In short, the aims of health units would be to make growth more perfect, decay less rapid, death more remote, and life more vigorous, happy and successful. The watchword is prevention.

speechtext:
As I said before, the

There have been many instances in the past where people were indifferent to or resisted health measures, but in this case the country has been fortunate in having these proposals received with open arms, as far as I have been able to observe.

National Health
There are a few units in British Columbia, and of course that is the way we must start. Some hon. member asked a moment ago about the maritime provinces. I am afraid he is not here at the moment, but in this connection I may say that I am informed that some philanthropic organization, some large insurance company or in any case some organization desirous of doing good, has undertaken to finance two health units in Prince Edward Island, which will cover that province. Not long ago it was announced that the province of Ontario proposed to institute health units, and while these plans are being held in abeyance at the moment I think the people of the province generally are looking forward to the organization and establishment of these units.
Within the last few years there has been a very considerable advance in this direction, and certainly there has been much evidence of the approval of the people and of health authorities. This is a sound, practical method of dealing with public health. Perhaps I should have mentioned also that in the United States, where this work was started before it was begun in Canada, there are something over four hundred units at the present time:
It seems to me that these health units very well might be called rural health units, because I think their great usefulness is in the rural districts. Cities of any size have health units to-day, many of which are doing excellent work, but the rural population is not supplied to any extent with the protection and comfort of these health measures. It has been thought desirable, not only from the standpoint of health but for the good of the country, to offer this protection and comfort to the rural population so that they may enjoy the advantages which are afforded the people living in cities. Other things being equal, one would have reason to suppose that the health of the rural community would be better than that of the city, but that is not the case. I think the obvious explanation is that health measures are not available in the country to the same extent that they are available in the cities, and the health measures of the city are sufficient to overcome the advantages of the pure air and sunshine of the country.
There is one thing we should not forget, and that is that these health units may be of great advantage in maternity welfare. Of course they will do good work in connection with contagious diseases and so on, but maternity welfare is going on, or should be going on all the time, no matter how healthy a community may be. Unfortunately, in the country the care given mothers must be very in-22110-108
adequate, and I believe this method may do a great deal towards meeting this very important need.
As hon. members are aware, these units are composed of four or five individuals; there is a health officer, a sanitary inspector, one or two trained nurses and perhaps a clerk. The great advantage lies in the fact that there is a full time health officer. The day has gone when we .can depend on any general practitioner being an efficient health officer. The work is too great and the advances in public health are too frequent to enable us to look for efficiency in public health matters in a general practitioner.
I do not think we need over-emphasize this matter of health units; there is no doubt they are very excellent things. The question is how to establish them. As the mover of this resolution has pointed out, this subject has received the warm support of the present Prime Minister, and I am sure his opinions have not changed in this regard. We have had several very important health matters discussed in this house during the session, and hon. members will notice from the order paper that there are still others to be considered. Mr. Speaker, I have no intention! of saying more than a very few words on this subject because there seems to be complete unanimity in the house. Several facts stand out as definite and as being accepted by this house. The first is that the maintenance of public health, both by preventive and curative measures is essential for the nation. The second is that there is perhaps mo better method of ensuring that health than by means of health units, particularly so in the sparsely settled districts where it has been found very difficult to provide medical and hospital attention. This is a matter which the public in one capacity or another should support. When I say the public, I mean in a financial sense as municipalities, provinces or the federal government. Every effort should be made to avoid wastage and to assure that the proper results are reached. Every method of coordination should be used, and one definite plan should be adopted from one end of the country to the other. To achieve that end we must have the financial cooperation of the municipalities, who have a certain definite responsibility and who understand as no other authority can understand the peculiar circumstances of each particular case; we must have the cooperation of the provinces with their knowledge on a wider scale of the necessities of their particular districts, and as germs and disease know no provincial boundaries, any more than they can be kept closed in by the wire fences of any particular municipality, we must have some federal cooperation expressed in the terms of financial assistance. In my opinion the one practical step which should be taken at the moment is that when such a conference is held, as has been suggested by the minister, and when the matter is discussed, it would be not only of value but almost essential that the different representatives in meeting should know exactly how the different authorities view this matter; that they should know whether in the plans which they may discuss and which they may be prepared to draw up, they may depend upon the effective support of all those three authorities, because the plans which they might lay at such a conference must rest

National Health
to a very large degree upon their knowledge of the attitude which the federal, provincial and municipal governments will take when these plans are put into effect. To that end I would again suggest it would be well for the house as it did a year ago, once more to express its opinion-I am not speaking about division or a recorded vote-and pronounce definitely by the acceptance of this resolution, thus giving assurance to those representatives when they meet, that when they draw up their plans they may depend again upon the definite sympathy and financial support of parliament as well as of the provincial and municipal authorities. Therefore I feel that this resolution should be accepted unanimously, and the government should continue to give that consideration which would enable them to supplement with effective support those plans at the time they are definitely drawn up.

speechtext:
The resolution before the house brings up a very interesting discussion of the whole question of health activities as they affect the federal government, provincial governments and municipal governments, the division of jurisdictions, and the degree of activity which should be pursued by the various governments, all pressing upon us the necessity for some definite decision, after proper conference, between the different governments in regard to the division of their jurisdictions. The other day when we were discussing the question of state medicine, preventive medicine was brought forward as one of the great functions of the state, and I for one am quite prepared that, as far as the resources of the country and as far as the financial resources of the various governments will permit, the state should stand behind preventive measures in connection with health activities.
When we come to the question of health units, we have one of the best efforts of scientific minds to-day in advancing preventive measures. Real undertakings in some of the provinces are being advanced. In the province from which I come, as an hon. member has already pointed out, two health units are being established, fairly well organized and ready to start functioning. I believe Ontario has announced a wider program and the provincial ministry of health intends to establish in different parts of the province health units carried out on a more extensive scale than is the case at present.

speechtext:
It is the only way in which effective results can be secured. The efforts of private physicians to treat the addicts to narcotic drugs is sure to meet with failure. At the present time the drug addicts in our province, and I presume it is the same in most of the provinces, are either given treatment in their homes by private physicians, or they are sent into the general hospitals for treatment, or as is done in our province, in some cases they are committed to a mental hospital-for treatment. Now in the great majority of the mental hospitals in this country, and in practically all of our general hospitals, there are no facilities for the proper treatment of drug addicts, and if any advance is to be made in their treatment there must bfe special institutions for their special treatment. The question at once arises, who shall provide those institutions? Shall it be the municipality, the provincial government or the federal government? Who shall provide for their maintenance? That is a proper question, I think, for discussion at such a conference as has been suggested.
May I go just a little further in regard to some of the difficulties that present themselves? To-day the question of caring for mental cases in all the provinces is becoming a tremendous task. It is a burden that is resting upon the taxpayers of our province almost beyond endurance. I am informed, and I believe it is correct, that there are more mental cases in the mental hospitals of Canada than there are patients in all the other general hospitals in this country put together. If that statement is correct it gives the house some idea of the problem that presents itself, and the sad feature is that the number of mental cases is increasing year by year. The question arises, are we going to 'be able in the provinces and in the municipalities to deal with the cases in the way that is required? Is the burden going to be carried as it has been carried in the past? Those again are questions that I think might properly come under the survey of the proposed conference.
If the federal government is going to enter further into health activities, may I in that connection point out that the greater portion Df the cost of sickness is included in the hospital costs. To-day most of our hospitals are finding their financing a great burden, which is becoming heavier every day. Heretofore the provinces have been giving grants, small as compared with the great work that has been done by the hospitals. If the highly expensive care of the patient which is given in our hospitals is to be continued and if the preventive medicine side of the work that

has been asked of our hospitals is to 'be extended, measures must be provided for the necessary financing. That again is a proper subject for discussion at the proposed conference.
Hence, Mr. Speaker, while I am in favour of any action by any government that would advance the cause of preventive medicine, whether it be the promotion of health units, greater activity in our health organizations in the municipalities, in the provinces or in the federal sphere, at the same time it seems to me that the problem is of such magnitude and such great importance that the federal government should very carefully deliberate just how it can be most effective in its assistance, and where financial assistance is given to preventive medicine, how it can be given most effectively, and where the jurisdiction should lie. All these considerations impress upon me the necessity of a conference between all the various governments and health organizations concerned with a view to arriving at the conclusion that will give the best results.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
On the 3rd day of March, 1930, this
house unanimously agreed to the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government	should	take	into	consideration	the
advisability of making grants to the provinces equal to one-third the cost of establishing, and to cover permanently such full time health units as may be organized.
The motion now before the house is:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government	should	take	into	consideration	theadvisability of carrying into effect the decision of parliament made on the 3rd March, 1930, to make	grants to the	provinces equal to	onethird of	cost of	establishing,	and to cover	permanently, such full time health units as may be organized.
In other words, the resolution is that the government should take into consideration the advisability of considering tbe advisability of taking the action in question. That is what it means. There is only one method by which that can be done, and that is by considering the matter with the provinces. To do that involves the discussion not only of the question of overlapping of effort, but the question of the extent to which effort should be made by the provinces and the Dominion and the character of the work which should be done by the health units, also the question of the financial burden that would be involved.
It is unquestioned that any effort that ensures the health of the people of this country adds to its national wealth. But it

National Health
is equally true that the direct measure of benefit in the first instance is largely through those branches of our activities that are covered by the ninety-second section of the British North America Act. I have not in any sense changed the opinion that I expressed formerly as to the desirability of making a very vigorous effort through the united endeavour of the Dominion and the provinces to ensure improved health conditions of the people of Canada, but I am certain that the mere adopting of a resolution in a new House of Commons, commendable though it is, will not accomplish that purpose any more than the passing of the resolution a year ago last March did accomplish it. But it does do this:	It directs public attention to the desirability of action being taken to induce the people to think in terms of preventive medicine, realizing the soundness of the old saying that prevention is better than cure.
If I were to take the time this afternoon, I could point out that already very considerable sums of money provided by the Dominion are being expended through the provinces, for this purpose. The hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Stanley) has referred to some of the work done in connection with the treatment of narcotic drug addicts. Hon. members will observe in the estimates that there are $100,000 being provided by the Dominion treasury for the benefit of social services rendered to health departments of the provinces. Contributions from the Dominion treasury bring up another matter mentioned by my hon. friend from Battle River (Mr. Spencer) concerning the desirability of maintaining some of the voluntary organizations which have done such excellent work in connection with the housing of public interest concerning the health of the people. From the very nature of things, in the end these voluntary organizations would go out of existence. Their effort is to arouse public opinion to such an extent that action is taken, and when necessary action has been taken the necessity for further effort on their part ceases. That has been the experience in connection with two or three such movements in the Dominion in the last twenty-five years. Groups of high-minded public-spirited citizens have organized as a voluntary association and as such have promoted public measures. Such measures have been promoted through educational effort, by the use of posters, by lectures and various other means. Private subscriptions have been made and in many instances these have been supplemented by grants from provinces and from the Dominion exchequer.

The result has been -that when public opinion has been aroused it has expressed itself in the manner by which the will of democracy is made known, namely by the enactment of legislation giving effect to the aims and purposes of the voluntary associations to which I have referred.
I need hardly say that is the British way by which reforms are accomplished. Those who will take the trouble to think back for a moment will realize that almost all great reforms, whether it be the load line on ships which we owe to the efforts of Samuel Plimsoll, the social reforms secured by Howard and Lord Shaftsbury, or the improvements of medical services and nursing in the army resulting from the efforts of Florence Nightingale, have come about through the voluntary effort and sometimes through months and years of toil on the part of those who have set up and maintained voluntary organizations for the purpose of creating a public opinion which would place upon the statute books of the country the desired -measures.
Measures to improve public health are based in the first place upon a selfish desire on the part of the state. It realizes that ultimately disease means loss, loss of earning power, loss from inability to create new wealth, loss through maintenance during periods of illness, loss to families sometimes resulting in poverty itself. To no inconsiderable extent the state has -been governed by selfish considerations. Such considerations may not be the most desirable in the world, yet they are those which in the end perhaps have weighed as highly as any other upon the minds of legislators themselves. Then there is the individual to be considered. There is the thought in every man that he should make so-me contribution to the welfare of the community in which he lives, and the taxes which he pays, and which after all constitute the revenue of the country, should be made useful and effective for the purpose of promoting health and happiness in those who have not been so fortunate. Sometimes the thought is prompted by an experience in connection with disease or illness. A person may thus have an earnest desire by preventive measures to make it impossible for others to become ill, and to ensure the freedom of others from the disease or illness from which he has suffered.
Let us consider the use of vaccines. Let us consider the problem of rendering the people of this country immune from disease. There are vaccines for many ills, antitoxins for typhoid and diphtheria, and in an indirect way the Dominion is constantly making con-
169S

National Health
tributions to health work. Health units go deeper than that; they go farther than that. They aim to create, if possible, a healthy community by commencing even in the prenatal days of the child, to ensure conditions which will bring about health in the citizen. From a time prior to the birth of the child and until he or she has attained manhood or womanhood and after, the health unit is in constant service. Consideration is thus given to the responsibility of the state for the health and happiness of the individual. Steps are taken first to prevent the recurrence of disease and ensure protection from centres of infection such as the teeth and tonsils. Children's diseases such as scarlet fever and measles are given consideration. Then when those children reach the teen age they are surrounded with conditions which will ensure their strength of body and mind to meet the problems of the life which lie before them. We are doing work along that line all the time. The Dominion is indirectly making its contribution to these health units. I believe it is possible to attain the operation of health units in every part of the country and in every part of this Dominion only through the joint action of federal and provincial authorities.
It is quite clear that in the realm of taxation, for instance, there must be a clearer understanding than heretofore there has been. It is not possible for the Dominion to raise money by any mode or process of taxation merely for the purpose of passing it on to the provinces, if before it is raised it is felt -that such money is raised for provincial purposes. If however for national ends the Dominion regards it as necessary that contributions should be made to further the efforts of the provinces carrying on their work within their more restricted areas, I think very little difficulty will be experienced. That of course involves very close study and consideration of the problem by provincial and Dominion authorities.
I need hardly say that, since August 7, this administration has not had the opportunity, owing to the conditions which prevail in this country, to call the conference it will call to deal not only with problems of taxation but also with problems concerning which there may be duplication of effort by the Dominion and the provinces. There is a federal health department. Most of the provinces have provincial health departments. It is quite clear that unless .there is a clear defining of the respective services to be carried on by
[Mr. Barnett.j
these departments there will be duplication of effort and loss caused through such' duplication. Early in his term of office I think it was contemplated by the Minister of National Health that he might be able to call a conference, but matters of more supreme importance in connection with the other branch of his department prevented such a conference. A conference was called which lasted but a day to deal with a constitutional matter. , Knowing that to deal with problems connected with taxation and activities over which both the Dominion and the provinces have jurisdiction, such as agriculture, health and matters of that kind, a conference will take several days, probably weeks; that some of those matters would involve an amendment to the constitution and others an agreement merely to define the work to be undertaken, we can agree only that this motion may pass as the motion last year passed. However I direct attention to the terms in which the motion is drawn, lest it should be said that the decision taken last year was a decision that meant more than the terms signify, and that the result of passing the resolution would be that this government is instructed by the house-as was the government that was in office before this administration-to take into consideration other than the advisability of carrying into effect the decision of parliament last year, which charged the then government to take into consideration the advisability of considering the establishment of full time health units, to the cost of which one-third was to be contributed by the federal authorities and two-thirds by the provincial . authorities. Without in any sense [DOT]committing the government as to the extent to which contribution may be made, or as to the terms under which assistance may be rendered, or as to when it may be possible to have the matter dealt with, because I can hold out no hopes that it can be dealt with this week or next week, this month or next month-without, I say, in any sense committing the administration to any of these details, we are quite content that the resolution should be unanimously adopted by the house; for the opinions that were expressed unanimously last session, are, I take it, still the unanimous opinions of the house.

But when the Minister of Health was asked by someone on this side whether it would be called this year, he intimated at once that possibly it would not be. I would have been much better satisfied had the Minister of Health or the Prime Minister been able to give us some definite idea when the conference will be called. We all know how easily these things are put off. If we could only have some promise that the conference will be called at the earliest opportunity, it would be something to look forward to. The Prime Minister mentioned that certain contributions are already being made by the federal government to the provinces in aid of health work. I would point out that so far as I am aware there is no new contribution being made this year beyond what was being made a year ago. I want, however, sincerely to thank the Prime Minister for the support which he has given to the resolution.
As to the wording of the resolution, under the rules of the house I had no other way of presenting it. I gladly accept the suggestion of the Prime Minister that the matter be left to a further conference, and I hope that that conference will be called at the earliest possible date.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE THE FARMER TO SECURE LOANS ON FAVOURABLE TERMS
PROPOSAL TO ENABLE THE FARMER TO SECURE LOANS ON FAVOURABLE TERMS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, consideration should be given to the setting up of a system of intermediate credits for agriculture.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, the statement is
heard repeatedly to-day that if Canada could find a satisfactory market for her wheat, we would speedily recover from the depression in which we are now involved. It is more readily recognized to-day than formerly that agriculture and industry are becoming more and more interdependent, and that one cannot continue to succeed at the expense of the other; both must march forward together. Up to the present time agriculture has not received proper consideration, in so far as
credit facilities are concerned, but has managed to carry on because of homestead and cheap fertile land. That period is past Conditions have so changed that no longer can the farmer be described as the most independent man on earth. To-day he is part and parcel of the great world industrial machine, and while our prairie farmer may be situated in the centre of the North American continent thousands of miles from the sea, he is as vitally interested in the daily reports of world happenings and conditions as is the individual in any other walk of life.
The farmer is being told to-day that he must reduce the cost of his production. I realize that that is true, but I believe I am right when I say that the Canadian farmer is faced with, greater handicaps in the matter of distance from markets and high interest rates than is the farmer in any other country. And yet I say without fear of contradiction that there is no country in which the per capita production is so great as in Canada, and it is my opinion that there is no one thing that would go further to assist the farmer to reduce his cost of production than lower interest rates. Dr. Tory, who gave a great deal of study to this question a few years ago, brought in a supplementary report in 1925 on Agricultural Credit, and I wish to quote a few excerpts along the line of the handicaps under which the farmer is labouring. On page 9 of that report Dr. Tory says:
It ought to be clear to anybody that Canada is slowly passing through the stage in her agricultural development that the United States was passing through some years ago, viz., the best lands of the country have been taken up, wealth accumulating from the rise in land prices will, in a large measure cease, and land mortgages based on growing prices will be harder to carry.
Further on he says:
In addition, he finds himself in competition in the markets of the world with countries where complete and ample financial organizations have been created for agricultural purposes. For example, in all the countries of western Europe capital is obtainable at a rate not exceeding 5 per cent and current money at similar rates. This has been brought about by special legislation in the interest of agriculture.
Again, he says:
The distances from the markets of the world also place the western provinces and to a limited degree the eastern provinces also at a great disadvantage.
My object, Mr. Speaker, in moving this resolution, is not to get any special privilege for the farmer, nor to get what might be termed easy money, but rather for the pur-
Agricultural Credits

pose of placing agriculture more on an equality with other industries in so far as securing legitimate credit is concerned. Europe recognized this question years ago and dealt with it. The United States recognized it almost twenty years ago, and the government sent a very able commission to Europe to study the various systems of agricultural credit, and later they introduced a very comprehensive plan to deal with the matter. With the permission of the house I should like to quote from a speech made by Harvie Jordan, a member of the commission.
Jhe governments of every European country which our commission visited took the broad position that the strongest foundation upon wu}ch any great nation could be built was one which was supported by a progressive, happy, and contented agricultural population.
From this standpoint the governments of the best agricultural countries of Europe have for the past half century given every possible cooperation and assistance to the development of their agricultural industry.
It is a singular fact in this connection, that while foreign farmers secure their borrowed capital at 4 per cent per annum, the average rate of interest on commercial loans for the same countries is from 5 to 6 per cent.
[DOT]	condition of affairs is just the reverse
in the United States. Our merchants, manufacturers, and railway corporations secure loans at from 5 to 6 per cent, while the average rate of interest charged our farmers is from 9 to 10 per cent. Not only this, the government of the United States has for the past 50 years bent its best efforts, energies, and powerful influences, through the enactment of federal legislation, to foster and protect the great industrial businesses of the nation, leaving American agriculture to carve its way along as best it could.
In the establishment of the national banking system of this country farm lands were outlawed by federal enactment as a class of security upon which loans should not be negotiated. Yet it must be admitted that the safest and highest class of gilt edge securities m the nation to-day are its improved farm lands, upon which the government, the people, and all other industries of the nation must depend for support and progress.
That statement applies equally to Canada to-day. It is not my purpose at this time to criticize our banking system. I believe it has been excellent for the needs it was designed to meet, but in its present form it does not and cannot adequately serve the present day needs of agriculture. It is my opinion that the average business man does not fully realize the change that has taken place in agricultural conditions during the past thirty or forty years, and the urgent need for credit to-day as compared with former times. I believe a better understanding of this question by the urban dweller would work to the benefit of all concerned.
TMr. Lucas.]
Just here I should like to quote from one of the other commissioners, Mr. Gordon Jones:
Let us keep in mind, in our discussion of this subject, the relative importance of the citj' and the country. Destroy the city and the country surrounding it would soon rebuild that city, but destroy the country surrounding a city and the city could not rebuild the country, but of itself could not long survive. The more prosperous the country, the greater and more prosperous the city, and as the city becomes greater and more prosperous it is stronger position to render financial assistance to the country. As the city increases its manufacturing output and enlarges its industrial activities, its population of consumers increases and a greater market is thereby made for the products of the country. There is indeed an interlocking of interest and a consequent need of "cooperation" between the city and country, and the best results can only be obtained by a spirit of harmony and proper understanding.
I wish I could impress forcibly upon every member of this house the importance of that statement. Let me say to our manufacturers and our business and professional men, if you want to help yourselves, the quickest and surest way to do it is through the farmer. It is a well known fact that when agriculture is prosperous so likewise are other industries.
With regard to the changed conditions of agriculture, no greater proof can be offered than to recall to those hon. members who, through the courtesy of the International Harvester Company, witnessed a short time ago a moving picture entitled Romance of the Reaper, an illustration of the development of the machinery of production from 1831 down to the present time. But, Mr. Speaker, while lalbour-saving machinery has solved the problem of production and removed from farming a great deal of the drudgery and hard work, it has brought in its train other problems equally important and, I believe, more far-reaching in their consequences which must be faced to-day. I refer to the problems of finance and distribution. While the introduction of machinery has increased production and taken much of the drudgery out of farming, the present method of financing, with high interest rates, has more than offset this benefit. I believe that to-day the farmer is more of a slave than he was in former times, but in a different way; for it is a trite saying that work never killed a man but worry did. When I think of the state of mind of the vast majority of farmers in western Canada to-day because of the staggering burden of interest they are carrying, with very little hope of ever getting out from under, I cannot help but admire the courage and fortitude with which they are carrying on.

Agricultural Credits
I feel confident, Mr. Speaker, that if the same energy, the same intelligence and determination were applied to the solution of the credit problem as have been applied to scientific and technical questions, equal success would result. Sir Josiah Stamp, who is recognized as one of the outstanding British economists, is reported to have made the statement that science and invention might well take a holiday for twenty years, and he proposed that business men and financiers should give more time t-o the study of elementary economics.
The problems and difficulties with which we are faced at the .present time are man-made problems. They are not caused by lack of raw materials or by our inability to convert those raw materials into usable form; rather the reverse is the case. I am convinced that since man has created this .problem man can solve it, if only he will set himself seriously to the task. As I said before, Europe has dealt with the question of agricultural credit, and in Germany and France we have perhaps the two outstanding rural credit systems, by which money can be obtained at very low rates of interest.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE THE FARMER TO SECURE LOANS ON FAVOURABLE TERMS
speechtext: And Italy.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE THE FARMER TO SECURE LOANS ON FAVOURABLE TERMS
speechtext:
Yes, Italy as well. In 1894 France passed the first fundamental law creating machinery for the provision of agricultural credit. Two years later, when the charter privilege of the Bank of France expired, it was renewed by the government only on condition that the bank should advance to the government forty million francs, free of interest, to be used in the subsidization of the rural credit banks. There was a further condition that the bank was to pay yearly a sum calculated at one-eighth of its circulation, but not to be 'less than two million francs, to be used for the same purpose. In reality this has amounted to between five and six million francs yearly, and this amount has been made available for agricultural credit. Loans are made to agricultural cooperative societies, with interest as low as 2 per cent. Let me pause here, Mr. Speaker, to say it might be well to insert a clause of this nature when we revise our Bank Act in 1933.
Just here I should like to read another short excerpt from the report of the United States commission:
Our rural population is justly entitled to receive credit direct from reserve banks in the same degree that urban population enjoys this advantage; and the method of bank organization should be such that residents of country districts can successfully overcome the disadvantages of their environment.
The general advice given the farmer today is to go in for mixed farming. I have tried to point out that credit is just as essential in agriculture as in any other industry. Our present banking system serves admirably the needs of industry and commerce, but it does not serve the present day needs of agriculture, though it is true that our banks do provide a certain amount of short term credit. It is also true that in 1926, after repeated urgings from this corner of the house, parliament passed the Farm Loan Act for the purpose of providing long term credit for farmers. There is however a gap between these two systems which might be termed intermediate credit, and with this my resolution proposes to deal. I refer to a system of credit for periods of from six months to three years.
Everyone who understands the needs of agriculture knows that a bank loan for from three to six months is of very little use to the man engaged in live stock production. It takes from one to two years, and sometimes even longer, properly to mature cattle, and under present conditions the farmer often finds that he is forced to throw his stock on the market at a time when it is not fully matured and often when prices are depressed. The very fact that Mr. Beatty, along with other financial interests, has seen fit to promote the Dominion Agricultural Credit Corporation Limited to supply the very form of credit I am suggesting, if I understand it correctly, is an added proof that there is such a need. I am confident, however, that the capitalisation of that corporation, which is $5,000,000, will prove totally inadequate to meet the needs, and I would suggest to the government that if they cannot see their way clear to set up an intermediate credit system of their own in competition with the private corporation, at least they cooperate with the Beatty plan by subscribing dollar for dollar. This will not only give financial support but will add to the importance of the organization and assure its permanence as an integral part of our financial structure rather than as an emergency measure. I think it will be admitted that this new corporation, backed by business interests such as these, would be carefully supervised and managed along strictly business lines, and with these precautions the government should be prepared to take a risk equal to that taken by private capital for the benefit of agriculture.
A few days ago, the right hon. the Prime Minister, speaking on the question of a central bank, quoted President Hoover as saying:
It is not possible for the debtor to borrow himself out of debt.
Agricultural Credits

While that statement taken by itself may be true, under our system where the large percentage of business is run on credit, it is or should be possible to borrow money at a reasonable rate of interest and by using that money in legitimate business, along with energy and skill, make sufficient profit to repay the loan and at the same time reduce the original indebtedness. That is the theory upon which business is conducted to-day and it was with that end in view that I introduced this resolution in the hope that a better system of credit might be evolved which would place agriculture in the same position as that which other industries now occupy in this respect. The' question of intermediate credits was introduced in a very able manner last year by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) and after debate was referred to the banking and commerce committee for further consideration. Unfortunately parliament dissolved soon afterwards and the matter was not dealt with. I trust this question may at least be referred to this committee for consideration, for it is my opininn that if agriculture is to survive it will require wholehearted cooperation of every interest in the country in the matter of working out a better and cheaper form of credit.
It is not my intention to debate this question further, but I hope the house will give to it the consideration which it merits.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO ENABLE THE FARMER TO SECURE LOANS ON FAVOURABLE TERMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members were pleased with the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the spirit in which he has received this resolution. After a very few remarks, I will move the amendment which he suggests.

While I am on my feet, I should like to say that this matter of credit for agriculture is one which should be settled as soon as possible. I intend to discuss this question from the viewpoint of a westerner because I am most familiar with the western situation. Western Canada has been settled by a body of men many of whom never borrowed any money in their lives until they went to that district. They were not familiar with any credit system under which they could borrow, but they have been educated by the agents of the mortgage companies and of the banks to do their business on credit. The moment they secured a recommendation for a patent for their homestead they were solicited by the agents, particularly of the mortgage corporations, to borrow money in order to improve their farms. From that time on they have done a large percentage of their business on credit. Perhaps there is nothing strange in that, because ninety per cent of the business in this country is carried on on a credit basis, but no attempt has been made to evolve a system of credit suitable to agriculture, particularly in western Canada, although I think the same remark would apply to the east.
Bankers have appeared before the committee on banking and commerce and have told us that the Bank Act contemplates that the business which they do should be only the financing of industry by the granting of short term loans, and I believe that that Is the intention of the act. The mortgage companies do not pretend to finance farmers except for long terms, and it has been generally admitted that there always is what the bankers term a barren area of credit. It is true that in many cases the bankers in western Canada have financed the farmer, and I agree with a recent statement by one of the past presidents of the Canadian Bankers' Association that the banks have loaned too much money to farmers in the west. That statement may be true, but the responsibility rests largely upon the banks themselves. I must be fair and state that this would apply only to certain banks; I have no desire to indict the bankers as a whole. The farmers could not have obtained these large loans unless the banks had been willing to grant them.
What the farmer needs is a system of credit which will be fairly constant, one which will not advance him more credit than he needs at certain times and withhold it at other times when he is badly in need of it. That is the trouble with the present credit system

Agricultural Credits
in western Canada; it makes credit much too easy to get at certain times. On many occasions farmers have been urged by local bank managers to borrow money for purposes for which they should never have borrowed it, and as a result many farmers have suffered. I have personal knowledge of men being persuaded to go into the ranching business. The local managers assured them that the banks would advance them sufficient money for the purpose, and what happened? The banks had to take security on everything they had, and before many years had passed the value of live stock dropped to such an extent that these men had to be sold out. That is not a proper banking policy; the Bank Act never contemplated that the banks of this country should go into that kind of business.
I think it is time we had in Canada a proper system of credit for agriculture. I do not like to come to parliament and criticize the action of the banks in any particular part of Canada, but the criticism which we have already heard this session proves the need of a system better suited to the requirements of the agricultural industry. I do not desire to take up the time of the house in a discussion of why the banks in western Canada have lost so much money- a point stressed by the bankers' association- but I do want to say that if they have lost money in western Canada it was their own fault. They have taken huge sums out of western Canada in the form of interest, and if they have lost money it is because of the poor policy they have followed in making their loans.
I want to quote very briefly from the report of the committee on banking and commerce of last year with reference to the matter of agricultural credits, which was referred to them. They say:
Two sessions of the committee were held, [DOT] during which this reference was under discussion.
As directed in the order of reference, the committee conducted a study of intermediate credits for agriculture, but owing to pressure of other work they have not been able to give it the attention so important a subject deserves.
Hr. C. S. Tompkins, the Inspector of Banks, was examined and requested to obtain sundry information.
It is recognized by the committee that the basic industry of agriculture is handicapped for want of such credit facilities as are called for by the resolution.
it is true that short term loans are taken care of by the banking system, and those covering long terms more or less by the Long Term Loan Act, and mortgage companies; but that, with the slow turnover of the farmers' business, the third type of credits as mentioned above is essential to his success.
Your committee, therefore, recommend that the subject is of sufficient importance that the matter be given attention by the Department of Finance, and if possible, bring it to the attention of a future parliament.
In the last paragraph of this report it is stated that the matter was to be brought to the attention of the Department of Finance. Officials of that department were asked to obtain certain information in regard to it, so that they should now have information which would be available to the committee in considering the matter. Therefore, without taking up any further time of the house, I would move:
That the motion be amended by adding the following words:
"and to that end that this question be referred to the select standing^ committee on banking and commerce, with instructions to consider and report thereon."
Mr. ALFRED'SPEAKM AN (Red Deer): The house will be as happy as I that the general acceptance of the motion as amended renders it unnecessary for me to say what I had intended to say. There are, however, three or four points which I wish to lay before the house in reference to the scope of this inquiry
By the proposed reference the committee on banking and commerce will be afforded an opportunity of carrying on an inquiry veiy essential at the present time, having to do with the credit system of this country as it applies to agriculture. The committee will have an opportunity not only of considering the motion itself, but of acquiring a better understanding of the proposed operation of what is popularly referred to as the Beatty plan, of which very little is at present known but concerning which vague surmises are floating throughout the country. It would br of benefit to the originators of the plan, to Canada and to agriculture, if that system were properly understood. But still more important, the committee will be given an opportunity of inquiring into another very important aspect of the matter, namely the present relationship between the banks and agriculture in Canada. It is not good for the banks, for agriculture or for the country generally that such a dispute as has now arisen should continue. Many statements and accusations have been made, and it is apparent that a complete misunderstanding and misapprehension prevails throughout Canada, particularly amongst those engaged in agriculture, as to the functions of our banking system as related to agriculture.
I hope that the motion will be understood in its broadest terms and that the scope of
Technical Education

the inquiry will be fairly wide. It is desirable that this misunderstanding be thoroughly cleared up so that we may be able to ascertain definitely and without peradventure whether the banks have been functioning as they should, whether the demands made by agriculture have been reasonable or unreasonable, and whether the statement made by the heads of the banks that credit has been given in the usual way and on the usual security is correct or not.
The committee will have an opportunity of perhaps recreating our credit system as it relates to that important branch of industry, agriculture, of obtaining a better and more complete understanding of the situation as it exists, of setting at rest much ill feeling, much misunderstanding, and of bringing about a greater degree of friendly cooperation between these two essential units in our whole social organization, finance and agriculture.
Motion as amended agreed to.

subtopic: PROPOSED CONTINUANCE OP FEDERAL GRANT FOR ANOTHER TEN YEARS
PROPOSED CONTINUANCE OP FEDERAL GRANT FOR ANOTHER TEN YEARS
speechtext:
Whereas the discontinuance of the federal grant in aid of technical education has imposed a heavy liability upon the provinces, which they find it difficult to sustain;
And whereas the future industrial and commercial development of Canada depend in large measure upon the creation of a well trained personnel;
Therefore be it resolved-that, in the opinion of this house, the grant should be continued at least for another ten years.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution which I now propose to the house has been on the order paper for the last four years. It is needless for me to say that it has always been defeated. Perhaps this year it will meet a different fate. I am not going to utilize the forty minutes allowed to me according to the rules of the House of Commons. I shall be very brief; indeed, I do not believe my remarks will last more than five or six minutes. My motivating reason for curtailing my remarks on this very important subject emanates from the very sympathetic speech that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) made when the resolution was before the house last year as well as from the intimation in the speech from the throne that something would be done this year for technical education. Pending a statement from the Prime Minister as to the government policy with respect to technical education, I shall, as I have said, not utilize

my whole time but shall be as brief as possible.
In presenting this resolution I am absolutely certain that I am reopening a question that is not only of extreme importance to a very large proportion of the population of Canada but is also very closely connected with the welfare and prosperity of this Dominion, namely, federal government grants to technical education to aid industrial development.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that the latter part of the resolution calls for a continuance of the technical education grant for a further period of ten years, implying that such a grant has been in effect during some previous period. How was technical education legislation first placed on the statute books of Canada, and what were the events leading up to that legislation? Hon. members are no doubt aware that technical education always has been and always will be a vital question in a country with such great potentialities in trade and commerce as Canada. For almost half a century this question has agitated the minds not only of those who direct our industries but also of those who are engaged in them. It has, in a word, been a most vital subject in those quarters where the need for skilled workmanship was found to be essential. Indeed, so rapid was the growth of public opinion in favour of more and better technical education that it soon became apparent that it was only a question of time when the matter would come up for discussion in the House of Commons. That anticipated discussion did come up some time in the year 1909, in which year a royal commission was appointed to investigate the whole subject of technical education. The commission consisted of seven members, who visited many parts of Europe, and the United States and held over one hundred meetings in the Dominion of Canada alone. When you consider, Mr. Speaker, that over 1,400 witnesses were heard in Canada alone, and that the total expense bill of the commission was somewhere in the neighbourhood of $100,000, you will have some idea of the tremendous task which the commission had on its hands, a task that took about three years of investigation and study before the commission was finally in a position to submit its report to the House of Commons in 1913. In 1914 the great world war broke out and the matter was left in abeyance until after the armistice was signed. It was not long, however, before parliament took the question up with renewed vigour, which finally culminated in the act of 1919, now known as the Technical Education Act. That act provided for the expenditure of an aggregate sum of $10,000,000 over a period of

Export Act
ten years, to be paid to the provinces according to a graduated scale, as follows: in 1920, $700,000; 1921, $800,000; 1922, $900,000; 1923, $1,000,000; 1924, $1,100,000; and a like sum for each of the five succeeding years, ending with the fiscal year 1929. The sum of $10,000 was to be paid in each year to the government of each province and the remainder of the appropriation was to be allotted and paid in proportion to the population of each province respectively as determined by the last federal decennial census.
The money has been paid, Mr. Speaker, but the act is no longer available. The federal technical educational grants have been relegated, at least by the government that preceded this one, to the junk pile of forgotten things. I conclude with the hope that the present government will not relegate this act, as it was relegated last year, to the junk pile of forgotten things, but that it will take action to aid in the development of technical education as was intimated in the speech from the throne.
