MOTION FOR REPEAL AND NEGOTIATION OF TREATT IN SUBSTITUTION THEREFOR
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the statute entitled An Act to amend the Export Act, being chapter 19, 20-21, George Y, passed during the first session of 1930, should be repealed, and in substitution therefor a treaty should be negotiated for which Canada will get something in return for the loss of revenue this country is suffering in consequence of our good-will gesture, which apparently United States does not appreciate.
He said:	When the bill to amend the
Export Act was passed by parliament on March 25, 1930, strong objection was raised on the ground that Canada should get something by way of treaty in return for the loss of revenue, and also the loss of legitimate business in this country. In this connection I might quote from the remarks that were made by hon. gentlemen now sitting in this house. The right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), then leader of the opposition, at page 630 of Hansard of March 14, 1930, said:
We have failed to avail ourselves of one of the greatest offers that could be made by one nation to another, namely, to make reciprocal the operations of a treaty. They say, you give us this, we will give you the same. Moreover, sir, I might again point out that the proper method of international contract is by treaty or convention. As I pointed out a moment ago, this parliament cannot legislate for the United States of America. The United States Secretary of State said: Let us make a new convention amending the old convention.
The hon. the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) is reported at page 873 of Hansard of March 24, 1930, as follows:
It seems to me that if the mind of the Prime Minister radically changed in August last, as I understand it did, then there was ample time for him to negotiate an amendment to that treaty under which reciprocal duties and obligations would be imposed upon the governments of the two countries. It seems to me that such a treaty would have been far more consistent with the self-respect and dignity of this country than to place ourselves in the position. as seems to be the view of many of the leading newspapers of the United States, where we have been compelled to pass legislation because of the insistent demands of the United States that we should do so.
And again at page 875,1 find the following:
Therefore I say that we should have either a reciprocal agreement in the form of a treaty or some form of reciprocal legislation, which would give to Canada the same protection from smugglers from the United States as the United States now ask us to give with respect to smugglers of Canadian products into the United States.
In Hansard of March 24, 1930, pages 875-6, the present Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion) is reported as follows:
I entirely agree with him (the member for St. Lawrenee-St. George) who took exactly the same attitude, that in justice to Canada we might well have preceeded by way of reciprocal legislation, either a treaty or a convention, or concurrent legislation as suggested by the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George, because in that way we could have obtained for Canada some rights in return for what we are now giving up at the request of the United States.
And further at page 876:
"In other words the Post (Washington) asks what does Canada get for giving up this revenue and for the loss to private interest in this business, and for the extra expenditure which
Export Act

will be put upon. this country by this legislation? What is the quid pro quo? Do we get anything in return, or are we to draw the conclusion that this legislation, like the Prime Minister's tariff legislation, is a made-in- Washington policy, or a don't-provoke-Washington policy-not a Canadian measure, but a United States measure?
The right hon. the leader of the opposition, the then Prime Minister, is reported at page 909 of Hansard of March 24, 1930, as follows:

, I wish to place on Hansard a quotation from the Toronto Mail and Empire. This is a report of an interview with Clarence Darrow, the famous criminal lawyer of Chicago:
Darrow Sees No Need For Export Ban United States Rich "Enough to Take Care Of Its Own Laws," He Asserts Is Visiting Toronto
England Should Not Pay War Debts To Republic, He Contends
Toronto, July 26.-Canada should not concern itself with preventing liquor from being exported to the United States, Clarence Darrow, famous criminal lawyer of the United States and anti-prohibitionist, stated in an interview here. "The United States is quite wealthy enough to take care of its own laws," he said.
"So Much Richer"
"Why should Canada spend it9 money when the United States is so much richer and can better afford the expense?" continued Mr. Darrow.
On the question of war debts, Mr. Darrow declared England should never have taken on herself the payment of war debts to the United States. "We were in the same war," he said, "and we should help to pay for it. If it is not the debt of the United States, we should never have been in the war."
"I am awfully sorry for England," Mr. Darrow said. "She has packed up the whole expense of the war. Her debt should be cancelled, for she has fought the world's battles.
I wish to make reference to the Wickersham report, which caused considerable comment throughout the United States and Canada. At page 25 of this report I find the following:
It would be a mistake to assume that the cutting off of clearances of liquor from Canada to the United States has achieved its helpful intention.

If this is the conclusion arrived at in the United States after two years of investigation by the National Commission on Law Observance and Enforcement why continue the ban on exports to the United States? What have we received in return for Canada's gesture of neighbourly good will? First there was the Hawley-Smoot tariff, which as hon. members know prevented nearly all our agricultural and dairy products from entering the United States. That tariff legislation affected my constituency very seriously. Thanks, however, to the efforts of the present government and the new dumping clauses, the farmers and, market gardeners in my riding are happy and contended to know they have a home market and that the surplus products of the United States will not be dumped here in competition with our products.
Then there is the commuter problem, a very serious matter in my constituency and in other border points of the Dominion of Canada. On April 1, 1927 a joint agreement was negotiated by the Hon. Vincent Massey entitled General Order No. 86, which for the information of the house I should like to place on Hansard. I may say that very few Canadians seem to understand what the general order meant. During 1930 this order practically became null and void. Thousands of residents of the border cities had paid their head tax and the cost of their vises. Mr. Speaker, I trust that the house will not hesitate to give its approval to this resolution. In my opinion, farmers whose cattle have been subjected to the tuberculin test, in Quebec or throughout the country, for the last four or five years, did not receive an indemnity proportionate to the valuation of the cattle slaughtered. It was in 1927 that we inaugurated in the county of St. Johns-Iberville, which is situated south of the St. Lawrence, the tuberculin test. The highest price paid for cattle worth at least $100, was $38. I therefore think that the farmer was not sufficiently compensated for the losses he sustained, and that we should increase the indemnity from $60 to $90 as proposed, and from $150 to $180 for thoroughbreds. The remuneration for cattle that undergo the tuberculin test and are slaughtered, is only two-thirds of their valuation. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) could verify this statement by looking over the statistics in his possession. Most of the cattle I think which were slaughtered, at least in my county and to my knowledge, have never been paid, on an average, more than $30. You will readily understand that it is difficult to apply a system for the tuberculin test. It has happened, in my own constituency, in the spring during April, May, June and July, after cows had been wintered and at least 8 or 9 dollars per month had
been spent per head, that farmers were obliged to slaughter them and only received $28 or $30 per head, althought the cows were in a fit condition to give good returns. In the present instance, I do not think that the government proved themselves generous, the act should be amended within the shortest delay possible because, as everybody knows, agriculture has already suffered too much. Mr. Speaker, I listened

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. I invite your attention to the terms of the motion now under discussion. Resolution No. 23 on the order paper is as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the compensation of $60 provided for each head of cattle, male or female, as stipulated in chapter
6.	section 14, subsection 2(a) of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, be raised to $90 and that the compensation of $150 stipulated in section 2(b) of the same section be raised to $180.
My objection is that if the resolution passed in its present form an expenditure of public money would be required. I am aware that opinions may be expressed by motions, but not on a motion sudh as the present one. Paragraph 358 in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms is in part as follows:
Motions advocating public expenditure, or the imposition of a charge, if the motion be framed in sufficiently abstract or general terms, can be entertained, and agreed to by the house.
The present resolution if passed, however, would express a positive opinion of the house that the action outlined in the resolution should be taken, and that the expenditures therein mentioned dhould foe made. I submit it is beyond the powers of any hon. member to place such a resolution before the house.

I should like to speak to the point of order raised by the minister. First I should like to know if the objection should not have come from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), who has the right to introduce such a measure. In Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms I find at page 63, paragraph 549, the following sentence:
The rule also applies to releasing or compounding any sum of money due to the crown and to the imposition of any state tax upon the people, but not to pecuniary penalties necessary to the operation of a bill.
If after a tuberculin test of an animal it is found necessary to slaughter it, to a certain extent a penalty is exacted by the department. For that reason I submit that the present resolution does not involve the expenditure of money but rather the increase of a penalty which already exists in a law on the statute book. I submit the point of order is not well taken. If the resolution involved expenditure. of money by the crown or any transaction of a monetary nature I would say the objection was well taken, and that a private member should not have brought the resolution before the house. But the present resolution, as I have stated, merely provides an increase in a penalty already imposed by a statute.

During the past five or six years resolutions of a similar nature have been brought before the house, and I think on some occasions a similar objection was taken to that now raised by the minister. For instance, there 'was a resolution proposing the expenditure of about
310,000,060 on highways, another for the expenditure of a large sum of money for technical education, and another for the relief of unemployment. Those resolutions all came before the house on previous occasions and the same point of order was raised. Probably in the strictest sense of the word the point is well taken, but on the other hand I think hon. members will agree that the usage and custom of late years has been to permit debate on such resolutions. Paragraph 55S in the rules which have been quoted states:
Motions advocating public expenditure, or the imposition of a charge, if the motion be framed in sufficiently abstract or general terms, can be entertained and agreed to by the house.
The resolution with which we are now dealing begins with the words: "That in the opinion of this house." The construction is of a general character; the house is not bound by the resolution. If passed it merely expresses an opinion.

raised by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) I was looking into the rules myself.

Whereas, the Dominion of Canada is a signatory to the articles of peace of the Treaties of Versailles, thereby subscribing to the principle of a maximum working day of eight hours;
Therefore be it resolved that this house is of the opinion that the government of Canada should take appropriate steps to ensure, throughout Canada, the fulfilment of our treaty obligations and conventions arising out of the peace treaty, relating to hours of work.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it will be noticed that this resolution does not direct the government to take any specific steps but to take appropriate steps to ensure throughout Canada a maximum working day of eight hours. No doubt lion, members will recall the treaty of peace signed at Versailles on June 38, 1919. Part XIII, known as the labour section, lays down certain principles governing a maximum working day and a maximum working week. That treaty was signed on behalf of Canada by the then Prime Minister, Sir Robert Borden. Arising out of the treaty a conference was held in Washington in October, 1919, and again the government of Canada was represented. At the conference the principle of the eight hour day was accepted and recommended to the respective governments of the several countries that were there interested and represented. For the information of the house I will read that section one of the Treaty of Versailles embodying the principle of the eight hour day:
Whereas the League of Nations has for its object the establishment of universal peace, and such a peace can be established only if it is based upon social justice;
And whereas conditions of labour exist involving such injustice, hardship and privation to large numbers of people as to produce unrest so great that the peace and harmony of the world are imperilled; and an improvement of those conditions is urgently required: as, for example, by the regulation of the hours of work, including the establishment of a maximum Avorking day and week, the regulation of the labour supply, the prevention of unemployment, the provision of an adequate living wage, the protection of the worker against sickness, disease and injury arising out of his employment, the protection of children, young persons and women, provision for old age and injury, protection of the interests of workers when employed in countries other than their own, recognition of the principle of freedom of association, the organization of vocational and technical education and other measures;
Whereas also the failure of any nation to adopt humane conditions of labour is an obstacle in the "way of other nations which desire to improve the conditions in their own countries:
The high contracting parties, moved by sentiments of justice and humanity, as well as by the desire to secure the permanent peace of the world, agree to the following:
Then follows chapter 1, dealing with the establishment of a permanent organization, which afterwards became known as the international labour organization. As I said, in October, 1919, arising out of that provision in the treaty of peace a conference was held at Washington. At that conference it was agreed that a majority of two-thirds of the delegates present should be necessary on the final vote for the adoption of the recommendations of the draft convention. It is evident that the matter was well thought out and discussed at length. The principal of the eight-hour day was adopted at Washington and the convention was referred to the different member countries for ratification. When the ratification of the convention was considered by the Canadian government there arose the question of conflicting federal and provincial jurisdiction. In some quarters it was contended that it was a Dominion matter inasmuch as the treaty had been signed by the Prime Minister of Canada. In other
1716	COMMONS
Treaty of Versailles-Eight Hour Day
quarters it was contended that it was a provincial matter under the British North America Act. So in 1925 the question of jurisdiction was submitted to the Supreme 'Court of Canada, which decided that the regulation of hours of labour came within the jurisdiction of the provincial authorities, but that of course the. Dominion government had sole jurisdiction over its own employees. In 1930 the federal government implemented its part of the convention by legislation as far as it was possible for it to go. On the 27th of March. 1930, there was passed an order in council, which in brief, gives the eight-hour day. to all Dominion employees. There was also passed an act respecting fair wages and the eight-hour day for labour employed on public works of the Dominion. This act was assented to on May 30, 1930. Representations have been made to the various provinces, from many quarters, that they should implement their part of the treaty.

of the industrial wage-earners is of supreme international importance, and that although differences of climate, habits and customs, economic principles and industrial traditions make strict uniformity in the conditions of labour difficult of immediate attainment, there are methods and principles for regulating labour conditions which all industrial communities should endeavour to apply, so far as their special circumstances will permit.
[Mr. Heenan.l
2.	That approval was expressed in the peace treaties of the principle of the eight hour working day.
3.	That a draft convention was adopted at the first session of the conference of the international labour organization (League of ^Nations) in 1919, to limit hours of work in industrial undertakings to eight hours per day.
4.	That the draft convention above mentioned was referred in 1924 to the select standing committee on industrial and international relations of the House of Commons of Canada for examination and report.
5.	That on the recommendation of the committee on industrial and international relations of the House of Commons, approved by the House of Commons, the draft convention of hours of work in industrial undertakings was referred by order in council to the Supreme Court of Canada, with a view to determining the jurisdiction of the federal and provincial authorities respectively, on this subject.
6.	That the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada contained the following declaration: "The subject matter is generally within the competence of the legislatures of the provinces, but the authority vested in these legislatures does not enable them to give the force of law to provisions such as those contained in the draft convention in relation to servants of the Dominion government, or to legislate for those parts of Canada which are not within the boundaries of a province."
That is to say, the legislatures could not legislate for territory under the jurisdiction of the Dominion government, or for Dominion public servants. I continue to read:
7.	That a report from the Civil Service Commission, which was submitted to Your Excellency in Council under date of February 16, 1925, showed that the standard daily hours of work of monthly rate employees in the government departments, are from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with an interval for luncheon, and a half holiday on Saturday, and that the standard hours of prevailing rate employees, numbering 1,576 in Ottawa and 18,2G4 outside Ottawa (of whom 12,247 were postmasters paid on percentage basis) are 44 hours per week, based on an eight hour day for five days and four hours, or a half holiday, on Saturday.
Certain exceptions to these standard hours of work were also noted in the report of the Civil Service Commission.
8.	That request has been made to the government for the granting of the eight hour day to its own employees.
9.	That it is desirable that the principle of the eight hour day should be applied to any branches of the public service of Canada in which it is not now observed.
Then comes the recommendation of the minister:
The minister accordingly recommends that, excepting' in cases where the work of employees is intermittent in character, or the application of this rule is not deemed to be practicable or in the public interest, the hours of work of any employees of the Dominion government who are still required to work more than eight hours daily be reduced to eight hours daily, with a half holiday on Saturday.
The committee concur in the foregoing recommendation, and submit the same for approval.

Treaty of Versailles-Eight Hour Day
So when that was approved by His Excellency in Council, every employee of the Dominion government was placed on tjhe eight hour day with the exception of those in connection with whom the minister would say it was not deemed to be practical or in the public interest. In other words, the employees of the Dominion government automatically went on the eight hour day the moment that order in council was passed, and it was then up to the different departments to say what was not practical or what was not in the public interest.

subtopic: PROPOSAL TO GIVE EFFECT TO PRINCIPLE OF EIGHT HOUR DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I have every sympathy with the hon. member who has

introduced the resolution (Mr. Heenan), I must say that it would have come with better grace had he taken action a year or two ago when he was Minister of Labour in a government which had the power to do the very thing he now proposes. However, it is well that he is at last converted to the necessity of fulfilling our obligations under the treaty. In fact I believe he has been converted to the necessity all along; it was a question of the government of which he was a member accepting his advice in this regard. Now that a new government is in office, I hope they will not dilly-dally until they are again in opposition before seeing the necessity of action.
We meet again with our old friend the British North America Act. I do not intend to traverse the ground covered the other day in the discussion which took place as to the necessity of Canada's having the power to amend her own constitution, but it would seem to me as a layman-I cannot say how it may seem to some of the legal minds in the house-that if Canada had the authority to sign a peace treaty she has a very definite responsibility to see that the terms of that treaty are carried out. We have been very censorious with regard to certain nations who have not fully lived up to their obligations under the peace treaty, but we must remember that the labour clauses of the peace treaty are just as solemn and just as binding as those which relate to boundaries, reparations, disarmament, and so on.
We have our responsibilities, and it was felt when these clauses were inserted, that labour, having suffered a great deal and having waived its claims during the war, had a right to certain consideration after the war was over. Therefore these labour clauses were inserted in the treaty. It must be remembered that unless we on our part live up to our obligations, it is going to be very difficult for other nations who signed the treaty, to live up to theirs. The idea was that we should have certain recognized standards pertaining to labour, and the eight hour day was amongst them. It would seem to me that in our British North America Act there is already ample provision to carry out our obligations under the treaty. There are certain residuary powers left to the Dominion, and I think we have fairly good judicial ground for saying that these residuary powers are sufficient to enable us to carry out our obligations.
The mover of the resolution made this statement:	"There is only one province that
implemented its obligations under the peace

Treaty of Versailles-Eight Hour Day
treaty." To me these words show the utter absurdity of the present position. No one province has obligations under the peace treaty. It was not a province that made the war; it was not a province that signed the treaty. It was the Dominion that went to war; it was the Dominion that signed the treaty that brought the war to an end, and it is the Dominion and not an individual province that is responsible. Therefore we do not get anywhere by assuming that any province has obligations under the treaty. It is we as a Dominion who signed the treaty and it is we as a Dominion who should hold ourselves responsible for implementing the clauses in the treaty. I cannot help thinking after all it is because organized labour in Canada is comparatively weak that we have had such a long delay in carrying out these clauses in the peace treaty.
The fact is that until very recently we have had a considerable number of employees in the public service who have beeen working more than the eight hour day, and I believe there are still some in the public service who are working longer hours. Someone has called my attention to the fact that we have persons in the postal service and so on who are in this position. I cannot very well believe any minister can take the ground that it is in the interest of the people of Canada that men should work longer hours.
Let me call attention also to the seamen, certain grades of whom are working ten and twelve hours a day. They are a class of men who should be considered as coming directly under the Dominion authority; certainly they do not come under any provincial authority, and yet no one so far as I am aware has made any effort to modify our shipping act so that the men who go down to the sea in ships should work only eight hours a day. This is something that comes directly under Dominion jurisdiction.
A year ago attention was called to a large number of people in Canada who were working not only eight and ten hours but even twelve hours a day, and during certain periods, twelve hours a day for seven days a week. Every hon. member who was here a year ago must recall the debates which took place in the house in connection with the steel schedules and the proposal that some of us put forward that increases in the tariff should be made contingent upon the adoption of the eight hour day in the steel works at Sault Ste. Marie and at Sydney. Somebody asks:	Who was the Minister of Labour
then? The Minister of Labour then was the mover of this resolution (Mr. Heenan). I do not want to press that too hard, because
not only did the government of that day refuse to do anything, but I recall that although the opposition gave us some support for a time, when the motion was actually pressed to a division they would not stand behind it. At that time we had a splendid opportunity of insisting that increases in the tariff should be made contingent upon the eight hour day, but it was not taken advantage of. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) promised, however, that unless changes were made within the year, the eight hour day would be enforced in the steel works. I understand some of the men have since been put on the eight hour day and some on a ten hour day, but no legislation has been brought into effect.
It is several years since the premier of one of the provinces wrote a letter urging the Dominion government to call an interprovincial conference at which this matter could be discussed and some uniform action taken. That request was not complied with by the late government. I would urge that the present government should call such a conference at an early date so that an understanding might be arrived at with regard to this matter. For example, as regards the steel workers it would be quite possible to have Ontario and Nova Scotia agree on the eight hour day proposal, and the other provinces would probably fall into line. Indeed it seems to be very late in the day that we in Canada should be discussing the desirability of adopting the eight hour day when economists almost all over the world are urging that it is necessary to have less than an eight hour day, to have a six hour day and possibly a five day week, if we are to overcome the present difficulty arising because of the large number who are unemployed. I recognize that unless concurrent legislation along other lines is passed, the eight hour day might work a hardship in some of the factories in Canada. There are some people engaged on piece work who are driven very hard on a very low wage and it is impossible for them during an eight hour day to make a sufficient wage to bring their standard of living up to anything like decency.

It has been suggested that they could be exempted. I would say no; rather side by side with the legislation for the eight hour day we ought to have minimum wage legislation which would make it impossible for any employer to hire men at less than a decent living wage. We are coming to that stage when we ought to regard men as at least of as great importance
1720	COMMONS
Treaty of Versailles-Eight Hour Day
as cattle and horses. If owners starve their cattle or horses, we summon them for cruelty; surely we ought to insist that employers, if they are going to hire employees at all, should pay them a decent living wage. If then we are to have an eight hour day in this country, we should have concurrent legislation providing for a minimum wage so that men would receive a total annual wage sufficient to support themselves and their families. As one studies the industrial life across the country, one realizes that we are facing a new situation. Hundreds of thousands of our citizens are unemployed; people are going without work for weeks and months in the year. We ought to distribute work more evenly, and so, if we are producing more, as we seem to be, than the people have the power to purchase, one of the next steps would be to cut down the hours, as has been suggested, to a six hour day and a five day week. The distribution of the work over a larger group, would enable industry to absorb many of the unemployed. Of course there again we would have to have such legislation as would ensure that a lessening of the number of hours per week would not mean a lowered wage. The time has come when we must give very serious consideration to the great industrial problem that is now facing us. We cannot simply drift along allowing some employers to overwork their men for a few months and then turn them adrift, and allowing other employers to put in machines and turn out thousands of employees without giving them any chance of getting a job at all. I thought that we were worse off in the west than they were in the east. Probably we are, but only a few minutes ago I was. talking to some gentlemen from Quebec who were telling me something of the conditions there. The same serious difficulties are beginning to develop in the east, with men drifting about on freight trains from city to city finding it impossible to get any sort of job at all. The resolution I know does not go beyond the implementing of our obligations under the peace treaty, but in view of the serious unemployment situation it seems to me that we ought to give more careful attention than ever before to the idea of a general limitation of hours of labour.
Further may I point out that we are holding back reform legislation in other countries? I can never read the information bulletins as sent out from the labour office at Geneva and observe how far behind the other nations Canada is without a sense of shame coming over me. Instead of being in the van, we are rather a drag on the wheels of progress.

I
hesitated to rise to my feet, Mr. Speaker, first of all because I had no desire to enter into this debate, and secondly because I was waiting in expectation that the established custom would be followed, and that some member representing the government would make a statement of policy on such an important matter. We had an illustration of that a few minutes ago when, after discussing a resolution that appeared to be perfectly in order, it was ruled out on a technicality. Nevertheless, these resolutions are (brought in because it is the only method the representatives of the people have of informing the government of the temper, feeling and desires of the people they represent

in these public matters. It is generally supposed-perhaps it is more honoured in the expression than in the actual fact-that some member of the cabinet, more particularly the one whose department is concerned, will at least attend in his place and give some expression of the policy or intentions of the government in the matter. I would not have got to my feet at all if we had heard some expression from the minister who I presume represents in this house the Minister of Labour who is in another chamber.
Something has been Said about the eight-hour day being in force in government departments throughout Canada. I am sorry that the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Plunkett) is not in his seat, because no doubt he would be able to tell me whether the conditions still exist wrhich I heard of a few months ago, of an employee of one of the government offices in Victoria working twelve hours a day and seven days a week and fifty-two weeks in the year. When some protest was made, a subordinate official in that department expressed the opinion that it was quite all right. I think he said that this employee got three weeks' holidays in the year, and that should suffice him. Suffice him, after working twelve hours a day, and seven days a week, fifty-two weeks in the year, except for the three weeks' holiday?
I recall some years ago, when the agitation first became more or less pressing for legislation to provide for old age pensions, the government of the day issued some kind of manifesto in which they admitted that they were pledged to carry out the provisions of the Treaty of Versailles or of- the conventions adopted at Washington, one of which was the one before us. Another related to old age pensions. In that manifesto the government said that they were fully seized of their responsibility in the matter, and they deemed that they had discharged their duty to the fullest extent of their ability and obligation by informing the various provinces that it was up to them. Then they washed their hands of the matter and were quite happy to leave it like that. As the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Woodsworth) said, they appeared to think that Canada had assumed no responsibility as a nation when she signed the treaty. But the pressure of public opinion, particularly labour opinion grew stronger and stronger, and by and by it was discovered that the Dominion did have some power in connection with some of these matters; that while they could not exclusively deal with such things they did have such power as would enable them to help and
assist the provinces in carrying out the obligations which, while technically provincial, were really in the upshot of a federal character. So legislation was brought down giving assistance to the provinces in carrying out at least one of the nation's obligations, and that was with regard to old age pensions. We all recall the objections that were raised by those who were then sitting on this side of the house, and how they pointed out how very unconstitutional it was for the federal government to take that action. It was butting into provincial matters, they said, and nothing but harm could come of it; it would be resented by the provinces and would lead to all kinds of disaster; it was going too far, on the one hand, and was not going to get anywhere, on the other. Since then, possibly in response to the pressure of public opinion, and possibly with some faint regard to the prospect of an election in the immediate future, we find that one of the big parties pledged itself, if not to grant 100 per cent of the old age pension, to grant 99 per cent; thereby admitting that they could from the first have assumed practically the whole obligation. So I hope that we are advancing step by step until finally we shall be able to adjust between the two contracting parties, the provinces and the Dominion, the carrying out of some of these obligations which up to the present, with very few exceptions, we have been decidedly ignoring.
As a nation we are ignoring our obligations. We boast of our nationality and we signed the treaty of Versailles as a nation, but we are not living up to the obligations we then assumed. The suggestion has been made, and very aptly I think, by both hon. members who preceded me, that there should be a conference called. In the absence of any light or leading on the part of the government I would again urge that the; conference be held. A meeting between the provinces and the Dominion is very urgently required to solve several matters, such as that of affording relief during the coming winter. Every day the authorities in the towns and cities in the province of British Columbia are passing resolutions demanding this conference and saying that it must be held to take care not only of the certainty of need of relief for the next winter but also of the relief actually needed at the present time. People do not realize that although we are in the middle of the so called busy season every city has a substantial problem of relief assistance on its hands. If such a conference as I suggested a few days ago was held, it would be an appropriate time for the Dominion government to lay before the provinces this aspect

of the case. Federal authorities might say at such a time that they were prepared to give with a liberal hand and might ask the provinces not to forget their obligation. They might say to the provinces "If we help you on the one hand, what will you do to carry out your obligations in connection with matters with which you are as deeply concerned as we?" Such a conference would afford an appropriate opportunity to make some reasonable negotiations with the different provinces who are not in a position to flout this government or to say that they will pay no attention to its recommendations.
Mention has been made of men working less than eight hours a day. There are now a large number of men working less than eight hours, many of them because of hard times and other through a sense of loyalty to their fellow workmen. They are willing to work shorter hours so that the work may be spread around. Some employers are taking advantage of the labour situation, requiring their men to work short hours and in return giving equally short wages. On the other hand there are many firms which have realized the gravity of the situation and in order to spread the work around have put the men not only on eight hour shifts but on six hour shifts, and in most cases the men cheerfully agreed in the attempt to help their fellow men in distress.
The last speaker (Mr. Woodsworth) mentioned the conditions in the steel works of the eastern provinces. Taken by and large the average employer, like the average worker, is a pretty decent man; he will not abuse his employees or take advantage of an unfortunate situation. I am speaking about the bulk of them. Of course there are some who are consciousless and disregard their obligations. There are some who would take advantage of their fellow beings for the sake of making a little money-at least they think they make a little more money, but perhaps they do not. Those men, however, for the sake of some slight pecuniary reward will, as it is stated in scripture, "grind the faces of the poor." Those numbers are comparatively small. It would seem wise for us by legislation to lend our weight to assist those men who are willing to do the right thing rather than handicap them by having to compete with men who are false to their God, their neighbour and themselves.
It has been alleged, and truly I believe, that our lack of action has given an excuse for similar lack of action in other countries.
I think one hon. member asked to what extent Canada had fallen short of the standards 
of other countries. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre answered in a general way, not having his data before him. I am in a similar position, in this connection I shall refer to the records of the labour conventions passed at the meetings of the League of Nations at Geneva. In passing I would remark I think it was a mistake that those resolutions were called "conventions." If they had been called "resolutions" the people would have understood that they were binding thmesleves to something. People have a vague idea of the meaning of the word "conventions", and they do not understand they are binding themselves to a solemn obligation and agreeing to do such and such a thing. If the word "treaty" had been used I think the position would hve been clearer and the actual contractional obligations would have been understood. I am speaking from memory and am subject to correction, but I think that the conventions dealing with labour situations throughout the world issued by the League of Nations at Geneva numbered about four hundred. I believe the exact figure was in the neighborhood of four hundred and thirty. The number to which Canada agreed was, I am sorry to say woefully few. I should not like to go on record as to how few, but I think the exact number was in the neighbourhood of thirty-five. So that no matter what other nations have done we have a long way to go before we overtake some of those nations which, as the hon. member for 'Winnipeg North Centre has said, have obligated themselves to carry out a large number of the conventions, and have done so. The debate is not closed, and in fairness, and with no intention to criticize the government, I would suggest that the minister give us a lead in the matter by outlining the intentions of the government, if any. We should know whether the government purposes to do anything or to disregard the matter. I think that hon. members should be taken into the confidence of the government. Many times during this session when questions have been asked on the orders of the day we have been told that here and now is not the moment to discuss such and such a matter. We have been given assurances, we have been promised that at some distant and unmentioned date declarations of policies would be made. I suggest that now one of those auspicious moments has arrived; the time seems to be ripe for the government to declare its policy on the subject which has been brought up for discussion. The high contracting parties in order to promote international cooperation and to achieve international peace and security by the acceptance of obligations not to resort to war. by the prescription of open, just and honourable relations between nations, by the firm establishment of the understandings of international lavas the actual rule of conduct among governments, and by the maintenance of justice and a scrupulous respect for all treaty obligations in the dealings of organized peoples with one another, agree to this covenant of the League of Nations.

No advance can be made in regard to the proposal embraced in this motion until an amendment to the British North America Act has been passed.
My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition said that it is the duty of this government to take such a position in regard to this matter that it can speak to the provinces with force and effect. My view is that the provinces value their rights and their privileges under our constitutional charter just as highly as we in this parliament value ours, and the moment this parliament seeks to speak to the provincial authorities with force and effect, trouble is bound to ensue. We sometimes forget that our constitutional charter is just as much the constitutional charter of the provinces as it is of the Dominion, and they value it just as highly. The question involved in this motion is one as between employer and employee. It is a question of hours of labour, purely and simply, a question of civil rights, and questions of civil rights are expressly stated in the British North America Act to be within the legislative jurisdiction of the provinces. I assume that no one knows better than the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition that this matter has been determined by the highest tribunal in the land. From the year 1921, when the government of my right hon. friend took power, down to 1924, neither he nor his government nor his then Minister of Labour made a move or took a step in regard to the implementing of any obligations in respect

The question was put up squarely to the Supreme Court of Canada in 1925. I have not the report of the case before me, but I quote from the order in council referred to by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, as follows: __ That the judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada contained the following declaration: "The subject matter is generally within the competence of the legislatures of the provinces but the authority vested in these legislatures does not enable them to give the force of law to provisions such as those contained in the draft convention in relation to servants of the Dominion government, or to legislate for those parts of Canada which are not within the boundaries of a province."
That was the answer of the supreme court, and that answer portrays a real difficulty. This parliament is powerless to carry out a convention applicable to the Dominion of Canada save only in respect of our own employees. While the provinces agreed to adopt any obligations which were cast upon Canada by that treaty, the country and the house are aware that there is a clause in the British North America Act, clause 132, which is applicable to international treaties. That clause reads as follows:
The parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British Empire, towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries.
That clause enables this parliament only to deal with foreign treaties so far as national rights and interests are concerned, and does not give us the power in any way to dispose of, to impose upon or to limit the rights, duties or privileges of any of the provinces.
As I view this motion in the form in which it is moved I can see no objection whatever to its adoption at the present time by parliament. Speaking on another motion a week ago I stated that it was the intention of the government at some time in the not too distant future to summon a provincial conference for the express purpose of considering questions relating to the amending of the British North America Act. I realize and we all know that there is throughout the provinces of Canada a very strong desire that certain amendments should be made to our constitutional act; in fact requests in this regard do come from time to time, both from the east and from the west, particularly in regard to matters of taxation.
There is another question which will occasion a distinct cleavage between provincial and Dominion authority. I do not know that there is any right more sacredly held in the provinces of Canada than their right to legislate on all matters pertaining to property and civil rights. I would not be one who would dictate or seek to dictate to any province as to what line of action it should take in regard to matters distinctly under provincial control. I would not be one who would seek to speak with that force and effect which my right hon. friend mentioned we would have if we took a lead in regard to this matter. I realize that this question is one which the provinces themselves will have to decide, and if they are willing that in regard to this matter of civil rights, hours of labour and employment in the provinces, the federal government shall represent them in carrying out this convention, all well and good. On behalf of the government I say that we agree, but I shall be no party to dictating to or coercing the provinces in this or any other respect upon a matter which lies purely within provincial jurisdiction.

speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend for a moment? I think he is placing upon my words a construction that they were certainly not intended to have. If by "force and effect," he means compulsion, I quite agree with him that the Dominion has no right in any way to attempt to compel the provinces to do anything. But if by " force and effect" is meant what I meant, "speaking with some degree of authority," or if we put it the other way, "not without some force or without effect," as would be the case if our own skirts were clean, then that would be the interpretation.

I cannot agree that we
could speak with authority in this matter because the authority is not in the hands of this parliament. The authority to legislate in this matter is in the hands of the provinces. I repeat: If the provinces will agree, the way is made plain for us in this parliament; but if the provinces fail of agreement, there is no way of coercing them and you cannot get an amendment to the British North America Act to give you authority to coerce them unless the provinces agree that such an amendment be made. That is the practical, the whole difficulty. There is no use in beating about the bush. No one knows the difficulty better than the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He is a student of these matters; he has a very wide knowledge of them; he speaks with great authority upon this question, but he realizes just as fully as I do or as any other hon. member does that there is this real practical difficulty ahead of us. But I am willing to say that when the conference is called this is one of the matters which may fairly be submitted to it. For my part I would much rather that the provinces themselves introduced such a question. I know they will introduce at such a conference many other questions which affect their rights and some which involve ours; but I believe the best way to reach a conclusion, and a satisfactory one, upon this and many other questions, is to have that conference and to have it just as soon as it can conveniently be held.
The motion is a pious aspiration in the right direction and I think the house may well agree that it should carry in its present form.

speechtext:
I
am glad to hear the statement just made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie). At the present time there is no question of greater importance than that of the hours of labour worked in industry. Under the circumstances it is far better that the federal authorities take

the lead in this matter than that we wait until the nine different provinces do so. It is much easier for the central authority to assume the lead than to wait until the nine provinces can come together on common ground.
The question of hours of labour has ramifications outside the provincial aspect. The hours of labour in one country naturally affect the hours of labour in another, and the hours of labour worked in one province affect the hours of labour worked in another. In exactly the same way, as the acting Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) pointed out, when Ontario introduced the Workmen's Compensation Act in that province, other provinces in the Dominion followed suit. So it is with the hours of labour. I am satisfied that ultimately the hours of labour will have to be regulated, not merely provineially or federally, but internationally. For one country to be on an eight hour day schedule and another to be on a twelve hour day schedule is unfair, because it is obvious that a country where long hours are worked and the wages are low will find it much easier to compete with a country where there is a high standard of living. That is one of the reasons given why some countries cannot reduce the hours of labour or give increased remuneration to the workers engaged in industry.
I contend, therefore, that the federal government ought to make every possible effort to strengthen the League of Nations in its attempt to bring about international legislation along the lines indicated here this evening. Already several nations have carried out the recommendations of the League of Nations, not merely by adopting resolutions but actually by passing legislation. Amongst the countries which have adopted the eight hour day are Belgium, Bulgaria, Greece, Portugal, Rou-mania, Czechoslovakia and several others. In addition there are several countries which as yet have not put through such legislation, but the eight hour day is more or less effective as it is throughout the whole of the British isles.
The question of the eight hour day is not a new one. It has been before the peoples of different parts of the world for many a long year. In fact, when members of the present government chided the opposition for being so slow in their activities, I want to point out that away back in 1919 a commission known as the Mathers commission was appointed by the then government. It toured the country and brought in a rather comprehensive report in regard to labour conditions and legislation.

Treaty of Versailles-Eight Hour Day
I should like to quote just one recommendation of that commission. Recommendation No. 52 reads:
In many industries in Canada the eight hour day has already been adopted, and it has been recognized by the Peace treaty. We recommend that it be established by law throughout Canada, with due regard for the above consideration. Such legislation should provide for a weekly rest of at least twenty-four hours which should include Sunday whenever practicable.
So that away back in the summer of 1919 we had a commission which, after it had toured the country, brought in a recommendation in favour of an eight hour day. From 1919 until the present time very little progress has been made in Canada with regard to implementing the recommendations of either the peace treaty or the Mathers commission of 1919.
I said a moment ago that the hours of labour would be far more effectively regulated by international convention than by national legislation. Therefore I believe that anything we can do in this house to strengthen the only body in existence at the present time that is dealing with this question, should have the sympathy of all concerned. The only body of an international character dealing with these matters is the League of Nations. I believe it should be our duty to strengthen the League of Nations, and the only way in which we can strengthen it is by this house bringing in legislation implementing the peace treaty of Versailles. I was very glad indeed, therefore, to hear the pronouncement this evening of the Minister of Justice, that a conference with the provincial governments will be called at an early day. I hope that when that conference meets the Dominion government will themselves take a firm stand and go on record as being in favour of the eight hour day, and when it has been approved by the provinces, I hope we shall then be in a position to carry out the recommendations of the peace treaty.

I hesitate at this late hour to rise and address the house but
the question of the eight-hour day was a very live issue in the constituency of Selkirk, which I have the honour to represent, and which is populated by so many working people. When I first saw this motion on the order paper I Thought it was remarkable that it should be proposed by the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr Heenan) in view of the conditions prevailing in my constituency in relation to a matter under the supervision of the late government. I refer to the fact that in the constituency of Selkirk there is a federal penitentiary at Stony. Mountain. I have not been able to understand just how it was, if the late administration was in favour of the eight-hour day, that they allowed the guards at that penitentiary to work in shifts of eleven and thirteen hours-and I may add that at the present time they are still working long hours. Many of them are returned soldiers drawing a pension for disability incurred on active service, and they are called upon to perform the task of keeping guard for eleven and sometimes thirteen hours a day. One who has had military service knows that a man who has been on guard for a period of four hours, and often less, is very much inclined to go to sleep and is not able to perform his duty adequately.
I was interested in the remark of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the effect that the provinces expected the Dominion to fulfil to the letter the wording of this resolution. If he realizes that the provinces expected the federal government to live up to the letter Of this resolution, how was it that in all the penal institutions of this country the late administration allowed the guards to work for periods of eleven and thirteen hours a day? That is one thing that I have never been able to understand.
In the province of Manitoba there is also a provincial penal institution at Headingly, a very large institution housing more inmates than the federal penitentiary. In this provincial institution they have been able to establish an eight-hour day for the guards, and I see no reason why the eight-hour day could not be established in our federal penal institution as well.
(Mr. Pouliot.]
This question of hours of labour is one which is agitating the mind of every thinking man in Canada at the present time. We all know that by specialization of functions men are able to accomplish more in a lesser period of time than they were heretofore. The great problem we are facing to-day is not that of efficiency of labour, is not that of the production of the largest quantity of goods in the shortest period of time at a minimum cost. It is the problem faced at the present time by every nation in the civilized world, that of the distribution of work. As indicated the other day by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) we have to a great extent solved the problem of production, but we have not solved the problem of distribution. If the late government was really in earnest in the matter of carrying out the terms of the peace treaty, it is remarkable that this conference was not called long ago. If the late government was really honestly endeavouring to -carry out the obligation of Canada to the other nations of the world, such a conference should have been held. I realize that if the resolution were adopted and the law of the land became such that in Canada the eight-hour day should be compulsory, a great hardship might be inflicted on many of our workers.
